gotchas: EventBridge notifications for S3 are OFF until you enable them in bucket properties.
Native S3 notification filters are prefix and suffix only — no wildcards in the middle, no size or metadata filtering.
Overlapping prefix configurations for the same event type are rejected outright.
S3 event delivery is at-least-once and unordered — the consumer must be idempotent either way.
SNS, SQS, and Lambda destinations need a resource policy allowing s3.amazonaws.com with aws:SourceArn / aws:SourceAccount conditions.
Enabling versioning changes which events fire (delete markers produce ObjectRemoved:DeleteMarkerCreated, not Delete).

concepts.name: EventBridge to Lambda to Systems Manager: rules, permissions, and why nothing fired
concepts.explain:
The standard remediation pipeline is: a service emits an event (or CloudWatch alarm, or Config non-compliance), an EventBridge rule matches it, and a target does the work — a Lambda function, an SSM Automation runbook, a Step Functions state machine, or an SNS topic. Two distinct permission models are involved and confusing them is the most common failure. Lambda needs a resource-based policy granting events.amazonaws.com permission to invoke it (AWS::Lambda::Permission in a template; the console adds it silently, the CLI and CloudFormation do not), and separately an execution role for what the function itself calls. Targets that EventBridge must call on your behalf — SSM Automation, Step Functions, ECS RunTask, Kinesis — need an IAM role attached to the target in the rule.
When a rule 'does not fire', check in this order: is the event on the bus you put the rule on (a service event may be on the default bus, an org event on a custom bus); does the pattern actually match (patterns are case sensitive, must mirror the JSON structure, and a field you omit is a wildcard while a field you get wrong is a miss); does the target have the right permission; and did delivery fail after matching, which shows up in the FailedInvocations metric rather than Invocations. Attach a DLQ to the target so failed deliveries are visible instead of silently dropped.
concepts.exam_tests: Phrasings: 'the rule shows matched events but the function is never invoked' (resource-based policy missing), 'the rule never matches' (event pattern or wrong bus), 'failed invocations are increasing' (target permission or throttling — add a DLQ), 'automatically restart the instance when the status check alarm fires' (alarm action or EventBridge to SSM Automation). Discriminating metric pairs: TriggeredRules vs Invocations vs FailedInvocations tell you exactly which of the three stages broke.

example.scenario: A CloudFormation-deployed EventBridge rule matches GuardDuty findings. The rule's TriggeredRules metric increments on every finding, but the Lambda target's Invocations metric stays at zero and no errors appear in the function's log group.
example.answer: Add an AWS::Lambda::Permission granting events.amazonaws.com lambda:InvokeFunction on that function with the rule ARN as SourceArn.
example.why: TriggeredRules incrementing proves the pattern matched, so the break is between EventBridge and the target, and a Lambda target is authorized by its resource-based policy rather than by the rule. Widening the function's execution role changes what the function may do, not who may invoke it — which is why the console-created equivalent works and the template-created one does not.

rows: Pattern mismatch or wrong event bus
Test the pattern against a real event sample; check the bus
Missing Lambda resource policy or target role
AWS::Lambda::Permission, or attach a target IAM role
Add a DLQ; fix the target; check the target role
Configure a target DLQ and alarm on its depth

gotchas: Event patterns are case sensitive and must match the JSON structure; an omitted field matches anything, a misspelled one matches nothing.
The console adds the Lambda resource policy for you; CLI and CloudFormation do not — this is the single most common 'it worked in the console' bug.
SSM Automation, Step Functions, and ECS targets require an IAM role on the rule target, not a resource policy.
EventBridge retries a failed delivery with a default maximum event age of 24 hours and up to 185 attempts before dropping it.
A rule created on a custom bus never sees AWS service events, which are delivered to the default bus.
CloudWatch alarm actions can call SSM Automation and create OpsItems directly — you do not always need an EventBridge rule in between.

concepts.name: Scheduling, orchestration, idempotency, and DLQs
concepts.explain:
There are three ways to run something on a schedule, and they are not equivalent. EventBridge Scheduler is the modern one: one-time or recurring, cron or rate, real time-zone support with daylight-saving handling, flexible time windows to spread load, an execution role per schedule, and direct invocation of over 270 AWS APIs without a Lambda in the middle. EventBridge scheduled rules are the older mechanism, UTC only. Maintenance Windows are the right answer when the schedule must also carry a duration, a cutoff, and node targeting — patching, in other words.
When the automation has more than one step, has to wait, needs branching, or needs a human approval, Step Functions beats a chain of Lambdas: it gives you built-in retry and catch per state, Wait states without paying for idle Lambda time, Map for fan-out, and direct SDK integrations so a step can call EC2 or SSM with no code. SSM Automation is the equivalent when every step is an operational action on nodes or AWS resources.
Two cross-cutting rules the exam applies everywhere: delivery is at-least-once, so every handler must be idempotent (check current state first, use a conditional write or a client token, key on the event ID); and every asynchronous hop needs a dead-letter queue — on the EventBridge target, on the Lambda async invocation, on the SQS queue via a redrive policy — or failures disappear silently.
concepts.exam_tests: Triggers: 'run at 02:00 local time including across daylight saving' (EventBridge Scheduler — scheduled rules are UTC), 'thousands of one-off schedules' (Scheduler), 'multi-step with retries and a manual approval' (Step Functions or SSM Automation with aws:approve), 'the remediation ran twice and created two snapshots' (idempotency), 'failures are not visible anywhere' (DLQ). Also: 'least operational overhead' plus 'call an AWS API on a schedule' points at Scheduler's direct API targets rather than a Lambda wrapper.

example.scenario: A nightly cleanup Lambda is invoked by an EventBridge rule. Some nights it runs twice and deletes more snapshots than intended, and when it throws, the failure is only discovered days later from a support ticket.
example.answer: Make the handler idempotent by keying on the event ID or by using a conditional check before deleting, and configure an on-failure destination or DLQ with an alarm on its depth.
example.why: EventBridge delivery is at-least-once, so duplicate invocations are expected behaviour rather than a bug to be prevented upstream. A DLQ plus an alarm converts an invisible failure into a paged signal, which retry-count tuning alone would never do.

Time-zone aware; rules are UTC only
Designed for high schedule counts with per-schedule roles
Patch or command inside a change window

gotchas: EventBridge scheduled rules run in UTC only; EventBridge Scheduler supports time zones and daylight saving.
Lambda asynchronous invocation retries twice by default with a maximum event age of 6 hours — configure an on-failure destination to capture the rest.
A DLQ on an EventBridge target catches delivery failures, not errors thrown inside a successfully invoked Lambda — you need both.
Step Functions Standard workflows give exactly-once execution semantics and full history; Express are at-least-once and cheaper for high volume.
Idempotency means checking current state, not counting invocations — describe before you act, or use a conditional write.
EventBridge Scheduler needs its own execution role; it does not inherit permissions from the rule model.

I can explain why sharing an encrypted AMI requires a customer managed KMS key and what deregistering does not delete.
I can state the difference between ECR basic and enhanced scanning in one sentence, and how long the ECR auth token lasts.
I can pick between Mappings, an SSM parameter type, and a dynamic reference for a value that changes per Region or must stay secret.
I can say what Ref returns for an S3 bucket, an EC2 instance, and an Elastic IP, and when I must use GetAtt instead.
I can explain why a stack delete fails with 'export in use' and what the only fix is.
I can distinguish DeletionPolicy, UpdateReplacePolicy, CreationPolicy, UpdatePolicy, stack policy, and termination protection by the moment each one fires.
I can say what the default DeletionPolicy is for an RDS DB instance.
